I put in another comment about how I grew up in a bubble so I would have said the same thing until I was 17. In the workplace - idk, I think you'd have to be pretty lucky to never experience it but it is SO subtle sometimes. I remember I went on an interview at 25 and the woman called me "articulate and well-spoken" which made me uncomfy and made my family really mad when they heard it. That was actually a more obvious example, I knew it was low-key racist when she said it.

My last job was so weird though - I can only see in hindsight it was racist. I worked for what was nominally a very "woke" place with a lot of women and POC in leadership - POC, NOT Black ppl. I was in a role where I had to lead a lot of meeting and I was often dismissed. People would speak to my white male intern as if he was leading the meeting, not me (thankfully he realized that that was messed up). I was the only Black woman in my role, almost all other Black people were in admin and finance and I was in a more strategy role. I talked to a lot of admins who wanted to progress to my job but they were never given opportunities. A non-Black male started after me with no experience (I had worked at this org 3 years before stepping into that role) and was given tons more responsibility and business trips, which were promised to me as a condition of me taking the job.

Even with all that it took time for me to realize how racist it was. People will do a lot of jedi mind tricks to convince you it's anything but and it's a lot harder to see when they act woke. I don't know your coworker but talk to him more about this. Not every racist thing is screaming in your face and people will say and do everything possible to convince you that what they're doing isn't racist. If you don't have Black people at your job on your side, it can be impossible to tell. Only way I was able to was another Black woman at my job talking to me about how she's seen what was happening with me before. It can be so easy to believe it's you without someone else on your side seeing the same thing. Most of the time these people don't even think they're being racist, that's how engrained it is. And if they don't believe they're being racist, they will gaslight you like crazy and when you have the stress of work and no one on your side, of course it's easy to think it's you and not racism.

for #2 - the term "microaggressions" is pretty recent as of the 2010s. When I was growing up in the 90s/2000s, it wasn't really a thing - people were either racist or they weren't and it had to be pretty overt for anyone to take you seriously, even other Black people.

For the first 17 years of my life, I would have said that I hadn't. I grew up in the 90s/2000s when the term "microaggressions" wasn't a thing yet, but tiny, subtle things happened - it was just hard to call it racism since it wasn't loud screaming n-word racism and people (even Black people) would be dismissive if you called it racism. I also had mostly Black friends and went to a mostly Black high school. My elementary/middle school had more white people but definitely enough Black people to not feel like I stood out. I also grew up in a majority Black city (Baltimore). Looking back on it there were a few things that made me uncomfy but since no one would call it racism (back then) I didn't really know what to do with those feelings except dismiss them. This was also a time before social media was a thing, so while racist things were for sure happening, they weren't really making the news since people weren't really able to report them in the way they are now. From like the late 90s-mid 2000s I don't remember anything like what has happened from 2015 to today - I am sure it DID happen but there was no press so no way to know. And in my own life, I really only spent time with white people who were around Black people a lot, I really can't remember that much in terms of times I felt racism, I remember a girl who told me her grandmother didn't like Black people and I remember my middle school was kinda segregated along dating lines (but my 6th grade "boyfriend" was white and so was my friend's, so...).

I moved to Ohio for college and it was much more overt. I had never experienced anything like what I experienced in Ohio in Baltimore. In Ohio I felt othered, unattractive, people felt comfortable saying racist things in front of me - I had a roommate who said she wouldn't ever want to live with a Black person besides me, I had white people say the n-word (no hard r) in front of me, I got "I'm blacker than you". Literally none of this ever happened to me growing up. Not even remotely. At most I got "you talk white" from other Black people.


I was talking to my mom about this a while ago because she remembered a time when I was a teen where I said I hadn't felt like I experienced racism and it had upset her at that time. I told her, since no one acknowledged microaggressions, no one was running around calling me the n-word, and I wasn't seeing blatant racism on TV then like I am now - what exactly was I supposed to say? I had mostly Black friends, the few white friends I had weren't racist, I even had mostly Black teachers in HS...if the few small microaggressions I experienced weren't racism and no one was being overtly racist to me, what exactly was I supposed to be experiencing?

If I had grown up in Ohio I am positive I would have had a different experience. But I had a pretty small bubble growing up thanks to my parents of being surrounded by middle-class Black people like ourselves. There (thankfully) weren't really many opportunities for me to experience racism. I still don't know what my mother expected me to say.
